This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Trump’s short-lived press ban
CNN, Politico, and MS NOW are back in the White House after a court order.
Welcome to The Logoff: The media outlets President Donald Trump banned from the White House last week are back.
What happened? Early on Thursday morning, a federal district court ruled that the White House had to immediately restore press credentials for CNN, Politico, and MS NOW and allow the outlets’ reporters back into the building.
The White House did, eventually — but only after multiple reporters were rebuffed over the course of the morning. They were allowed back in around noon, nearly 11 hours after the court’s order.
What’s the context? Trump announced the short-lived ban last week on Friday afternoon, writing that outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES” while covering him. He also threatened that additional outlets could be added to the ban.
Why did Trump want to ban journalists in the first place? Most recently, the White House line has been “national security”: On Monday, Trump accused reporters of “violat[ing] our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources.’”
On Thursday, however, Judge Timothy Kelly, a first-term Trump appointee, wrote that the White House offered “little to back up their asserted national security interest.” (According to the media newsletter Status, one of the “unknown sources” the White House was complaining about was none other than Vice President JD Vance, speaking to reporters on a press call.)
Trump himself has also suggested a simpler motive: Last week, he told reporters that “it’s really just cumulative stories of the last two years. You get sick of it.”
Is this the end of the case? Not yet. Thursday’s ruling was only a temporary restraining order, good for 14 days max, and Kelly has said that he “intends to rule expeditiously” on a more durable preliminary injunction. Trump has already promised to appeal in the extremely likely outcome that the ruling also goes against him.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
I found this Washington Post article breaking down whether you should get a Covid booster shot this fall extremely useful, and you might too.
Plus: Fat Bear Week is on, and it’s not too late to vote. You learn more and can meet some of the contestants here.
Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

sources.news_title: As judge temporarily restores White House press access, Obama characterizes Trump’s media ban as a larger ‘foundational’ issue with the free press
sources.text:
Reporters whose White House access was revoked after President Trump barred CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the grounds were allowed back into the complex on Thursday. According to CBS News, this happened after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued an order granting the outlets temporary relief, forcing senior Trump administration officials to restore their press credentials.
Before the ban was lifted, former President Barack Obama gave his thoughts on the media ban issued by Trump at an event at Salem State University in Massachusetts. According to CNN, he said he was not surprised by the decision. He also pointed to a lack of partisan criticism, noting, “You can’t do that and say that you are still living in a democracy.”
He also stated, “The free press, the idea that the government cannot discriminate against, or pick on, or bully, or exclude somebody because they don’t like the criticism that’s being leveled at them, that is a foundational issue. And so, I am not surprised that the current president wants to ban newscasts that are critical of him, because he’s that guy.” Obama also noted that the ban would get overturned, but that no one from the GOP stopped him. “That lack of guardrails is what I’m most concerned about.”
A shocking ban
The ban was reportedly initiated last week, with Trump stating it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” Per CBS, the director of White House press operations received a notice at 7:10 am to restore the journalists’ access. According to the Secret Service, the badges were reactivated around 9:07 AM, and the confiscated credentials were delivered to White House Operations staff at 9:45 AM.
This entire slow trickle-in reportedly happened while Trump was welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House for a state visit. Since many outlets had suspended most coverage in solidarity with CNN, the elaborate ceremonies Trump organized for Jinping weren’t broadcast by major U.S. television networks. This is especially unsurprising when you consider that CNN is part of the press pool that documents the president’s daily activities.
CBS reported that Kelly’s decision to reinstate access while the outlets challenged the ban was issued after midnight on Wednesday. He wrote an eight-page ruling stating that the news outlets are likely to succeed in showing their due process rights were violated, and further noted that the journalists weren’t given prior notice of the bans or an opportunity to challenge them.
Kelly also mentioned he is skeptical of the administration’s claim that the bans were motivated by national security concerns. He pointed out that nothing in the record predates the suit to suggest that the revocation of the hard passes was motivated by national security. He specifically noted that Mr. Trump focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of the reporting when he announced the ban.
Per NBC News, the DOJ had previously argued that access to the White House is a privilege, not a right. They claimed the outlets failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum. However, Judge Kelly didn’t seem convinced by these arguments. He noted that one of the standards of conduct cited by the White House is so vague that it hardly does the trick
The Justice Department is expected to appeal. Additionally, Trump has already indicated on Truth Social earlier in the week that he would turn to the appeals court if the ruling went against him.
Interestingly, it isn’t only a former president and a federal government calling Trump out. Per CNN, First Lady Melania Trump quietly took a different stance than her husband when her office formally approved CNN’s and Politico’s press credentials for her “Fostering the Future Together” coalition on Tuesday. This underscores how she often operates independently of her husband.
For now, the restraining order will remain in place for 14 days, and the free press is back on the job while the court considers longer-lasting relief.

sources.news_title: Some banned media organizations return to the White House after judge's order
sources.text:
(WASHINGTON) — Reporters and producers from news organizations that President Donald Trump barred from the White House were back on the grounds after a federal judge granted a temporary restraining order to restore their passes.
Earlier Thursday, the lawyer for media organizations requested an emergency hearing as early as Thursday, telling a federal judge that the government has “already repeatedly” violated his temporary restraining order after the three news organizations were denied entry into the White House earlier in the day.
“Defendants have already repeatedly violated the Court’s Order. Plaintiffs respectfully request that the Court set a hearing by videoconference or teleconference as soon as possible this morning,” Ted Boutrous wrote.
Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the government to respond to the plaintiffs’ notice of non-compliance by 12:30 p.m. ET Thursday.
In a declaration submitted by the White House in response to Kelly’s order, officials said that access had been restored as of 9:55 a.m. ET.
Around noon on Thursday, the outlets reported that they were beginning to be granted access to the White House grounds.
CNN reporter Betsy Klein, who had her hard pass taken on Saturday, and others, walked through a White House gate shortly after noon after her hard pass was given back to her. MSNOW correspondent Laura Barrón-López was also back on the campus Thursday afternoon.
Politico reported one of its reporters had also been granted access.
Earlier Thursday, Kelly granted CNN, Politico and MS NOW a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to restore the outlets’ hard-pass press credentials.
The order requires the defendants, excluding President Donald Trump, as well as their agents and representatives, to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the White House hard-pass press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
Kelly granted the media organizations’ request in the ongoing case Cable News Networks, Inc. v. Trump after their credentials were revoked on Sept. 18, according to the court order.
Kelly expressed skepticism about the Trump administration’s argument that the stories it cited as justification for revoking the outlets’ press credentials raised national security concerns.
Kelly described the stories identified by the administration as “routine” and said he was “skeptical” that the government’s stated interest in safeguarding national security was the actual motivation for revoking the hard passes. He also noted that Trump did not mention national security concerns when he announced the ban.
“Nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” Kelly said in the filing. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was “banning” Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting.”
In a hearing on Wednesday, Kelly signaled that he believes the White House failed to follow the process established by earlier court cases to terminate a reporter’s credential.
“I think it is fair to say that the process that the court laid out in those two cases – the circuit laid out in those two cases – wasn’t followed here,” he said.
Boutrous focused on that due process argument near the end of the hearing, telling the court that the White House’s “Alice in Wonderland process” for terminating the credentials is “arbitrary” and “irrational.”
“It’s not due process when there’s been a prejudgment of the issue. Clearly, that’s happened,” Boutrous said. “They’re going to keep playing games, moving the ball. That’s not due process.”
Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik argued that the notice the White House provided in letters sent after 10 p.m. Tuesday night, days after the ban took effect, was enough. He also suggested the outlets’ responses might convince Trump to change his mind about the ban.

sources.news_title: Trump folds as White house press returns
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s war with the press hit a temporary stalemate Thursday as a federal judge restored White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico for two weeks. Last Friday, the president banned the three outlets, calling them “fake news,” as their journalists reported being blocked from accessing the White House.
In response, CNN, MS Now and Politico sued, and the Trump administration launched “Trump TV,” which is essentially a livestream of speeches and other reruns that apparently almost no one is even watching. During this week’s U.N. General Assembly, before giving a speech in which Trump mulled the annihilation of Iran, the president snarled at a reporter for asking him a question.
“You should not be here,” Trump told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins. “You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Collins later said on air, “We never said we were never going to cover the president.”
Trump didn’t follow due process in the ban, according to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, who ordered the administration to restore their access as the case is litigated. Reporters from all three outlets thus began reporting at the White House again, but the move has raised questions of whether Trump could try again, this time following due process.
Gabe Rottman, vice president of policy at the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, told NPR “The White House facility doesn’t need to let journalists in … But once it does … it cannot exclude journalists or news organizations because it doesn’t like what they report.”

sources.news_title: Judge Blocks Trump’s ‘Ban’ on Three News Outlets
sources.text:
White House’s After-the-Fact Justification For Ban Falls Apart
Overnight, U.S. district court judge Timothy Kelly granted the temporary restraining order sought by three news organizations — MS NOW, Politico and CNN — that President Donald Trump had “banned” from the White House.
Kelly, a first-term Trump appointee, found that the White House’s assertion that the stories either “threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods,” left open “the possibility that all the stories fall into the later bucket, rather than the former.” The news organizations, he found, were likely to succeed in their arguments that the White House did not use any kind of process in deciding to revoke reporters’ access.
A further bit of absurdity surrounded the White House’s effort to show these reporters were up to no good. All three of the banned outlets got letters saying that they were “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues and publishing sensitive or classified information,” and noting their reliance on “anonymous sources”; the letters then included examples of stories it took issue with.
At least one of those stories, however, was based on a press call the White House set up, and that a White House aide told reporters to attribute to a “senior administration official.”
“The contents of this call are on background, attributable to a senior administration official,” an aide said, according to a recording of the call obtained by the Washington Post. “By remaining on the line, you agree to those terms.”
The media newsletter Status later reported that the “senior administration official” was none other than JD Vance himself.
This may seem odd, but this kind of stuff happens all the time. Government offices and agencies hold formal calls with the press, but ask that the information be kept on background — not attributed to a particular person. I’ve been on dozens of such calls. It’s a little weird that the vice president was the source in this case, and that he was described, somewhat misleadingly, as a “senior administration official.” But the relevant thing here is: These were not leaks jeopardizing national security. They were not leaks at all: the “anonymous source” was speaking at a carefully managed event set up by the White House itself.
This ridiculous twist is not mentioned in Kelly’s middle-of-the-night ruling, but it seems he was nonetheless unimpressed with the amount of due diligence that the White House put into its claims that reporters behaved inappropriately. He had a comical bit of analysis noting that the stories the White House deemed problematic don’t in any way support its solution of banning particular members of the White House Press Corps.
Defendants offer no declarations or other support—classified or unclassified—explaining how any of the reporting they identified in their letters to Plaintiffs damaged the national security. The declarations they do provide include general background about classified information, but the declarants are senior officials in the Department of Defense who have no direct knowledge of how reporters operate in the White House, or about any of the facts at issue here. And supplemental declarations filed by Plaintiffs show that, in most cases, the reporters who authored the stories Defendants identify in their letters did not even hold hard passes. In the remaining cases, Defendants afford no reason to believe that the reporter’s possession of the hard pass was integral to the stories identified.

The message also noted some students may no longer have anyone to care for them, per the Wichita Eagle. “Please help us keep our students safe and cared for,” it said.

sources.text:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists regained access to the White House on Thursday after a federal judge temporarily blocked President Donald Trump’s ban, ruling that the outlets were likely to succeed in showing their press credentials had been revoked without constitutionally adequate due process.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico returned to the White House grounds Thursday afternoon after a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to restore their credentials, bringing an end — at least temporarily — to a days-long standoff over presidential press access.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order early Thursday directing the administration to “immediately return, reinstate and restore” the outlets’ White House access for 14 days while their lawsuit proceeds. Kelly concluded that the organizations were likely to succeed in arguing that their credentials had been revoked without adequate due process.
The restoration did not happen immediately.
Reporters from all three organizations arrived at the White House Thursday morning and were initially denied entry despite Kelly’s order, prompting the outlets to seek an emergency court hearing. Kelly directed the administration to explain the apparent noncompliance before journalists were ultimately allowed back onto the grounds later in the day.
CNN White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins confirmed Thursday afternoon that she had regained access.
MS NOW likewise confirmed its journalists had been readmitted, while Politico reported that its access had also been restored.
The dispute began after Trump announced Sept. 18 that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would no longer be permitted on White House grounds. He accused the organizations of producing “fake news” and criticized their coverage of his administration. Their permanent White House credentials were subsequently deactivated, and reporters were turned away when they attempted to enter.
The three organizations sued Monday, arguing that the administration retaliated against them because of their reporting and violated their First and Fifth Amendment rights by revoking access without notice or an opportunity to challenge the decision.
The administration defended the restrictions in part on national security grounds and argued that access to the White House is a privilege rather than an unconditional right.
Kelly was unconvinced by the record presented to him.
“The court is skeptical — at least on this record — that defendants’ interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes,” he wrote.
Kelly noted that Trump himself had publicly focused on what he regarded as inaccurate and negative coverage when announcing the ban rather than identifying a national security concern.
“For one thing, nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” Kelly wrote. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting.”
The judge also found that the White House had not provided the journalists with sufficient notice of prohibited conduct or an opportunity to respond before taking away their credentials.
Kelly relied in part on existing D.C. Circuit precedent requiring procedural protections when White House press credentials are revoked. He said those precedents remain binding regardless of the administration’s contention that they were wrongly decided.
The press-access fight disrupted the longstanding White House pool system, under which a rotating group of journalists provides reports, photographs, audio and video from presidential events when space prevents the full press corps from attending.
After CNN was prevented from performing a scheduled television-pool assignment, other major television networks suspended presidential pool coverage in solidarity. Fox News, ABC, CBS and NBC were among the organizations participating in the protest, while the White House Correspondents’ Association condemned the exclusions.
The ban consequently affected more than the three targeted outlets. Because pool material is shared throughout the media, the dispute reduced independent audiovisual coverage available to news organizations across the country.
Kelly’s involvement also revived a dispute from Trump’s first term.
In 2018, Kelly ordered the White House to temporarily restore CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s press credential after the Trump administration revoked it following a contentious presidential news conference. That ruling similarly focused on due-process protections surrounding White House access.
Trump appeared aware before Thursday’s ruling that the current case could end with the outlets returning.
Asked Tuesday about the litigation, Trump said he would “probably” allow the three organizations back if the courts ruled against his administration.
The temporary order does not resolve the broader lawsuit.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico are still seeking a final ruling on whether the administration violated their constitutional rights and whether the White House may exclude news organizations because of their coverage. The administration can continue defending the policy as the case proceeds.
For Thursday, however, the immediate practical effect was clear: after several days reporting from outside the White House gates — and several hours in which the administration continued denying entry even after Kelly issued his order — the three organizations were once again allowed onto the grounds.

sources.news_title: 'No One Can Hear You': Trump Caves and Lets Banned Media Back In After Judge's Order — But Not Before His Chosen Press Humiliates Him on the Way Out
sources.text:
Donald Trump‘s fight to control who gets access to the White House just took another dramatic turn.
Days after the president barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, reporters from all three outlets were allowed back onto the grounds Thursday after a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to restore their access temporarily. The judge said the ban was likely unconstitutional.
The reversal did not happen smoothly.
Some journalists were initially turned away Thursday morning despite the court order, prompting the three news organizations to seek an emergency hearing before midday restored access.
And the timing could not be more awkward for Trump. His attempt to sideline major news organizations came just as his administration rolled out “Trump TV” and began relying more heavily on its own White House feed — only for persistent audio problems to make even some of the president’s handpicked media moments difficult to hear.
On Wednesday, Sept. 23, Trump attempted to give the world an update on the status of his new ballroom.
However, something in the air did its best to disrupt any conversation on the White House lawn.
The press that met him on hump day avoided asking the complicated questions. Instead, reporters gave him an alley-oop with a question about one of his favorite subjects.
A reporter asked the question directly: “Mr. President, ballroom update. Can you give us a ballroom update?”
“Everything is going up really fast. Go there today, take a look. And we’re very much ahead of schedule,” Trump replied.
Trump seemed eager to discuss his unfinished party space. He said construction was ahead of schedule, though the room would not be ready for Thursday’s dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, according to ABC News.
But an unexpected problem ruined the moment for him and the approved press. In the background, a loud ruckus appeared to be competing for airtime.
According to Time, the audio problems first became apparent on the same day as his streaming service’s launch.
That same day, the White House unveiled a new helipad. Marine One’s engines drowned out much of Trump’s speech on the White House feed. The sound was messed up.
The television pool typically provides microphones along with the footage. Without its crew, viewers struggled to hear the president, as ambient background noise drowned out his remarks for both television audiences and reporters at the scene.
The incident echoed sound and audio issues that had affected a recent outdoor interview.
Undeterred by the poor audio, Trump touted his upcoming Thursday dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping: “I wish we had it for tomorrow night, because we have a packed house tomorrow night for President Xi.”
The reporter followed up, “And who are some of the attendees that will be at the dinner tomorrow? Can you share with us?”
Trump offered categories rather than names.
“Everybody. Everybody. Everybody wanted to be here,” he said. “I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world, a lot more.”
He called it “the ultimate crowd” and said demand exceeded the available space. “I wish we had more seats. That’s the only problem.”
One person on Threads thought the questions were too easy.
“With the White House pool boycotting, Trump now has nothing but MAGA propagandists following him around, so he’s facing hard-hitting questions like ‘Ballroom update?'” the person wrote.
But the sound was a bigger part of the online discussion, as many struggled to hear him over the background noise.
“Why is it so loud?” one person asked. Another said, “Speak up, Piggy. No one can hear you.”
Yet, some suspect Trump will soon back down and remove the ban, stating, “He’s probably going to get bored of this. He needs to be seen as ‘strong’ by yelling at the “evil fake news.”
Five major news networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC — form the rotating television pool that supplies shared broadcast feeds across the national press corps. That technical infrastructure becomes crucial when tight security footprints or deafening Marine One engines threaten broadcast audio.
The muffled sound at the recent helipad ceremony underscored the system’s value, exposing how easily the White House’s internal feed fails without professional pool equipment.
Meanwhile, “TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station” promises a continuous stream of presidential highlights and administration updates. The administration will use this and fill the channel with the moments he wants to replay. Wednesday’s ballroom exchange gave him another one.
Trump wanted the ballroom update to dominate the story, but viewers were stuck on the noise. Handpicking reporters did little to solve the issue: even his own feed struggled to carry his voice over the roar of the presidential helicopter.
The president may control the ballroom guest list. Controlling the press has been a much louder failure.
We hope this story was worth your time. For over 14 years, Atlanta Black Star has stayed Black-owned and independently run. We didn't get here by waiting on ad budgets that were never built to prioritize us. Our readers did that.
Corporate support for Black media has always been thin. Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S. advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020. That's the backdrop. It's not why we're asking.
The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

If you are able to, a recurring contribution does more for us than a single one-time gift, because it lets us plan the next investigation instead of just the next invoice. It takes about 30 seconds, no long form, no account. Thank you for continuing to support independent journalism and freedom of the press.

sources.news_title: Top news outlets back at White House as judge orders Trump to lift ban
sources.text:
Reporters from three news outlets banned from the White House by U.S. President Donald Trump were back on the grounds Thursday afternoon, hours after a federal judge ordered the administration to reinstate their access.
On a chaotic day at the White House gates and in court, CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists were allowed back in by midday, after earlier issues gaining access.
It was the latest development in an extraordinary showdown between Trump and media outlets whose coverage he dislikes. And it played out during a heavy news cycle with Chinese leader Xi Jinping visiting with Trump and world leaders gathered for the United Nations General Assembly.
On Thursday morning, a Secret Service agent had confiscated the journalists' credentials, the news outlets said in a court filing asking for an immediate hearing to address what seemed to be the White House ignoring the court's order. The administration said in its own filing shortly after the reporters were allowed back in that it took the White House time to begin the process of reinstating badges.
Trump first announced he was banning the outlets Friday, assailing what he called "fake news." He later said their reporting was a risk to national security. The outlets argued in a joint lawsuit that the ban was a blatant violation of the First Amendment because it singled them out for the content of their coverage.
In his late-night ruling to temporarily strike down the ban, District Judge Timothy Kelly said the news outlets had met the legal thresholds to obtain a temporary restraining order, in effect for 14 days. Kelly said they were likely to succeed in showing their access had been revoked without due process.
"This is a high bar, but Plaintiffs have met it," he wrote.
Kelly – whom Trump nominated in 2017 and who ordered a CNN journalist's access restored in a similar case in 2018 – said the government must have clear standards for conduct that would lead to revoking a press pass. He called the standard of objectionable reporting outlined in letters that the White House sent the outlets "so vague it hardly does the trick."
The judge also made clear he did not buy the administration's argument that the news outlets' reporting endangered national security – and noted that Trump himself had not used that argument in the beginning, focusing solely on what he called negative coverage.
"Nothing in the record ... suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns," he wrote.
The ruling came after Kelly heard arguments in an emergency hearing Wednesday. Temporary restraining orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo pending a closer review of the case by the court.
"This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law," Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, said in an emailed statement. "We greatly appreciate the court's swift action."
Boutrous argued in the hearing that there was an urgent need for renewed access, saying that the ban caused irreparable harm to the outlets at a time of momentous news events. "We're at war. We have world leaders coming to Washington."
Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik, in his argument, reiterated the administration's point that the president has the right to choose who gets into the White House.
"Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Velchik said.
In arguing that Trump was not engaging in viewpoint discrimination – the government singling out specific media outlets for the content of what they say or publish – Velchik said the president had criticized other news organizations, but not banned them. He noted, for example, that Trump had called ABC "the worst."
He added: "The president should be able to take immediate action to protect national security."
In response, Boutrous said, "Suddenly it's a national security case," arguing that the president brought up that point only after the lawsuit was filed.
Trump "keeps proving our point," Boutrous said, describing how the president has consistently used negative coverage of him as justification for the ban.
Kelly seemed to agree, writing of the national security claim: "Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning' Plaintiffs from the White House – instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs' reporting."
In a filing Tuesday, administration lawyers detailed letters sent to each of the three news outlets that identified "a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents, including those that have threatened national security and spread falsehoods."
Among the incidents cited were: CNN reporting on "'top-secret' construction details related to the East Wing bunker"; MS NOW reporting "on an alleged leak investigation"; and Politico publishing "a document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements."
Politico's letter also included an incident in June of a report in which a "senior administration official ... granted anonymity" predicted whether a preliminary deal would end the conflict with Iran.
That item appeared to reference a background briefing set up by the White House, where an official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the administration itself. Several other outlets also reported the official's remarks.
The ban prompted other media outlets to take action in solidarity. The U.S. network press pool – consisting of the five major networks, including CNN – has suspended coverage of Trump pool events pending further notice.
The ruling did not address that rotating pool. After the hearing Wednesday, the networks continued to refuse to air footage of Trump without assurances that CNN would be permitted into the White House pool.
At Joint Base Andrews, where the president formally welcomed China's Xi, journalists from Fox News, CBS and NBC were present but not shooting video.
Other television outlets whose crews were present, according to signs on their tripods and cameras, were NewsNation, Newsmax, Right Side Broadcasting Network, One America News and LindellTV.
Ahead of Wednesday's hearing, an amicus brief was filed by other news groups, urging the court to immediately restore the three outlets' White House access.

Kelly was skeptical of that argument. CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed their lawsuit earlier this week, arguing that the administration violated both the First Amendment and the Fifth Amendment. Their attorneys said the outlets had been punished for their coverage without receiving adequate notice or a meaningful opportunity to challenge the decision beforehand.
Kelly’s ruling focused particularly on the due process argument. He cited previous federal appellate decisions establishing procedural protections for journalists whose White House credentials are revoked and concluded that the outlets had demonstrated enough likelihood of success to justify temporary relief.
The dispute continued Thursday morning even after the order was issued. Reporters from all three organizations said they were initially turned away when attempting to enter the White House, prompting their attorneys to request an emergency hearing and accuse the administration of failing to comply with Kelly’s ruling.
By around midday, journalists from CNN and MS NOW reported that they had regained access and had their credentials returned. Politico’s status was initially less clear as the legal teams continued addressing implementation of the court order.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico back at White House, hours after judge ordered Trump to lift ban
Summary
CNN, MS NOW and Politico returned to the White House grounds Thursday afternoon after a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to restore their access. The judge said the outlets were likely to succeed on their claims that their press passes were revoked without due process and that the government needed clear standards for revoking access. The case came amid arguments over whether the ban was retaliation for coverage or a national security measure.
Key Facts
- U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House to immediately return, reinstate and restore the three outlets’ access for a temporary restraining order lasting 14 days.
- Kelly said the outlets were likely to succeed in showing their press passes were revoked without due process and that the White House’s standard for objectionable reporting was too vague.
- The administration’s filing cited reporting incidents involving CNN, MS NOW and Politico, including stories about bunker construction details, an alleged leak investigation and White House ballroom funding.
- The outlets and the administration argued over whether the ban was viewpoint discrimination or a national security action, with Trump initially describing the outlets as fake news before later invoking national security.
NEW YORK — Reporters from three news outlets banned from White House by President Donald Trump were back on the grounds Thursday afternoon, hours after a federal judge ordered the administration to reinstate their access.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists were allowed back in the latest development in an extraordinary showdown between Trump and media outlets whose coverage he dislikes. It comes during a heavy news cycle with Chinese leader Xi Jinping visiting with Trump and world leaders gathered for the United Nations General Assembly.
Also Thursday, the news outlets had asked in a court filing for an immediate hearing to address their inability to access the White House grounds earlier in the day. The filing said a Secret Service agent had confiscated the journalists' credentials.
Trump first announced he was banning the outlets Friday, assailing what he called “fake news,” and only later arguing that their reporting was a risk to national security. The outlets argued in a joint lawsuit that the ban was a blatant violation of the First Amendment because it singled them out for the content of their coverage.
In his late-night ruling to temporarily strike down the ban, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the three outlets’ access. He said they had met the legal thresholds to obtain a temporary restraining order, in effect for 14 days, and were likely to succeed in showing that their press passes were revoked without due process.
“This is a high bar, but Plaintiffs have met it,” he wrote.
Kelly — whom Trump nominated in 2017 and who ordered a CNN journalist’s access restored in a similar case in 2018 — said the government must have clear standards for conduct that would lead to revoking a press pass. He called the standard of objectionable reporting outlined in letters that the White House sent the outlets “so vague it hardly does the trick.”
The judge also made clear he did not buy the administration’s argument that the news outlets’ reporting endangered national security — and noted that Trump himself had not used that argument in the beginning, focusing solely on what he called negative coverage.
“Nothing in the record... suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” he wrote.
The ruling came after Kelly heard arguments in an emergency hearing Wednesday. Temporary restraining orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo pending a closer review of the case by the court.
“This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law," Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, said in an emailed statement. "We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
The White House did not respond to emails from The Associated Press asking for comment on the order.
Attorneys debated access to the White House and any risk to national security
Boutrous argued in the hearing that there was an urgent need for renewed access, saying that the ban caused irreparable harm to the outlets at a time of momentous news events. “We’re at war. We have world leaders coming to Washington.”
Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik, in his argument, reiterated the administration’s point that the president has the right to choose who gets into the White House.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” Velchik said.
In arguing that Trump was not engaging in viewpoint discrimination — the government singling out specific media outlets for the content of what they say or publish — Velchik said the president had criticized other news organizations, but not banned them. He noted, for example, that Trump had called ABC “the worst."
He added: “The president should be able to take immediate action to protect national security."
In response, Boutrous said, “Suddenly it’s a national security case,” arguing that the president brought up that point only after the lawsuit was filed.
Trump “keeps proving our point,” Boutrous said, describing how the president has consistently used negative coverage of him as justification for the ban.
Kelly seemed to agree, writing of the national security claim: “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting.”
The Trump administration outlined ‘reporting incidents’ of each news outlet
In a filing Tuesday, administration lawyers detailed letters sent to each of the three news outlets that identified “a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents, including those that have threatened national security and spread falsehoods.”
Among the incidents cited were: CNN reporting on “‘top-secret’ construction details related to the East Wing bunker”; MS NOW reporting “on an alleged leak investigation”; and Politico publishing “a document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements.”
Politico’s letter also included an incident in June of a report in which a “senior administration official … granted anonymity” predicted whether a preliminary deal would end the conflict with Iran.
That item appeared to reference a background briefing set up by the White House, where an official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the administration itself. Several other outlets also reported the official’s remarks.
Major networks refrained from covering Trump for the media pool
The ban prompted other media outlets to take action in solidarity. The U.S. network press pool — consisting of the five major networks, including CNN — has suspended coverage of Trump pool events pending further notice.
The ruling did not address that rotating pool. After the hearing Wednesday, the networks continued to refuse to air footage of Trump without assurances that CNN would be permitted into the White House pool.
Journalists from Fox News, CBS and NBC were present but not shooting video at Joint Base Andrews, where the president formally welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Other television outlets whose crews were present, according to signs on their tripods and cameras, were NewsNation, Newsmax, Right Side Broadcasting Network, One America News and LindellTV.

WASHINGTON — U.S. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly early Thursday issued an order that temporarily blocks President Donald Trump’s ban of three news organizations from the White House.
Kelly, in the eight-page order, said that the White House must “immediately return, reinstate, and restore the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO that were revoked” Friday and over the weekend.
The White House, however, didn’t appear to be following the ruling as of 10 a.m. Eastern on Thursday, when attorneys representing the news organizations filed a brief asking the court to hold a videoconference meeting as soon as possible.
“This morning journalists from each of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO attempted to enter the White House and were turned away. A Secret Service agent confiscated the hard pass of journalists from all three organizations,” they wrote.
Micah Stopperich, director of White House press operations, declared in a court filing just before 12:30 p.m. Eastern that his team delivered the press badges to the entry gate at 9:55 a.m. Eastern to be distributed to members of the media who had them confiscated.
Kelly’s order will continue for 14 days while the case continues to be fought in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. Trump is scheduled to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House Thursday.
Although Trump has indicated he will appeal any court ruling on the matter, Kelly noted that temporary restraining orders are “generally unappealable.” He said he would schedule a hearing for motions for a preliminary injunction, which would last until the final outcome of the suit and could be appealed.
The case began Monday when the three news outlets sued the Trump administration for barring their reporters from entering the White House grounds.
The news organizations asked the district court to grant them either a temporary restraining order or a preliminary injunction that would require the White House to return the press passes, allowing the journalists to work from the complex once again.
Kelly, who was appointed by Trump during his first term, had heard arguments in the case on Wednesday and appeared skeptical at the time of Department of Justice arguments. In his ruling, he said it appeared likely that the news outlets would succeed with their claim that journalists were denied their due process rights before their passes were confiscated.
While the Department of Justice argued that earlier cases dealing with press access to the White House were wrongly decided in journalists’ favor, Kelly said that he was “bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop,” referring to earlier rulings by the appeals court.
Kelly in his order also expressed doubt about Department of Justice arguments that the ban was in response to concerns about articles that dealt with national security or classified information, saying DOJ “offered little” to back up that contention.
Some news articles cited by the administration as endangering national security were written by reporters who didn’t even have White House passes, he noted.
Trump did not mention national security in announcing the ban and “instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly said.
“For another—and simply put—the record lacks factual support for Defendants’ contention that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the Court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds,” Kelly said.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from States Newsroom.
Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr., the lawyer for the news outlets, praised the decision. “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law,” he said in a statement. “We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
Jennifer Shutt and Ashley Murray contributed to this report.

A federal judge has ordered the White House to immediately restore press access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, temporarily blocking President Donald Trump’s move to bar the outlets from covering him.
U.S. District Judge Tim Kelly issued the ruling early Thursday in a lawsuit the three news organizations filed jointly after Trump announced Friday that he was cutting off their access to the White House.
Trump had defended the ban by accusing the outlets of dishonest coverage. “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote when announcing the restriction, adding that “Other Fake News Media Outlets” could face similar treatment.
The three outlets argued the ban violated the First Amendment because it targeted them specifically over the content of their reporting.
The dispute prompted five U.S. broadcasters to suspend their participation in White House pool coverage, an arrangement in which one network films events and shares footage with all television outlets for the day. The move was seen as a rare show of solidarity with CNN.
According to the Associated Press, Kelly’s order directs the White House to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” access for the three outlets. He found they had met the legal standard required for a temporary restraining order, which will remain in effect for 14 days, and that they were likely to succeed in showing their press credentials had been revoked without due process.
“This is a high bar, but Plaintiffs have met it,” Kelly wrote.
Kelly, who was nominated to the bench by Trump in 2017, previously ordered a CNN journalist’s access restored in a similar dispute in 2018. He heard arguments in the current case on Wednesday.
A temporary restraining order is generally intended to preserve the existing situation while a court conducts a fuller review of the case.
The White House had not commented on the ruling as of Thursday, and the president’s lawyers may pursue further legal action.

Kelly said they had “shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim” of being barred without notice or chance to appeal.
Kelly leveled a “Temporary Restraining Order” to “remain in effect for 14 days, and the Court will set a schedule for expedited briefing on a motion for a preliminary injunction during that time. The Court will then be able to consider such a motion with additional time and on a fuller record.”

But on the Fifth Amendment claims, Kelly said this. Notice the allusion in one citation to the 2019 case against first Trump term carnival barker Brian Karem:
The merits of this claim are assessed in two steps: “the first asks whether there exists a liberty or property interest which has been interfered with by the State; the second examines whether the procedures attendant upon that deprivation were constitutionally sufficient.” Ky. Much of Wednesday afternoon’s hearing revolved around the administration’s official filing claiming the three outlets must be barred because of past reporting that threatened national security.
Kelly said not only were the stories cited “routine,” but this was “not so ‘extraordinary’ as to permit deviation from the ‘essential principle of due process’ that a deprivation of liberty ‘be proceeded by notice and opportunity for hearing.’”
This was perhaps the closest Kelly came to weighing in on the claims about press freedom (click “expand”):
The final two factors, the balance of the equities and the public interest, also favor Plaintiffs. These two factors “merge when the Government is the opposing party.” Pursuing Am.’s Greatness v. FEC, 831 F.3d 500, 511 (D.C. Cir. 2016) (citation omitted). As the Court has concluded, the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes likely violated their constitutional due process rights, and “enforcement of an unconstitutional law is always contrary to the public interest.” Karem, 960 F.3d at 668 (citation omitted). Moreover, Plaintiffs—and the public—have an abiding interest in maintaining the status quo ante given the importance of the free press, which “stands as one of the great interpreters between the government and the people.” Grosjean v. Am. Press. Co., 297 U.S. 233, 250 (1936).
On the other side, Defendants argue that revoking Plaintiffs’ hard passes and excluding them from the White House serves an important national security purpose, citing Defendants’ interest in “protecting classified and sensitive national security information.” No doubt, protection of the national security is a weighty interest on the Executive’s part...Still, on this record, Defendants offer little to back up their asserted national security interest to justify revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes.
“[T]he record lacks factual support for Defendants’ contention that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the Court orders their passes reinstated...Defendants offer no declarations or other support...explaining how any of the reporting they identified...damaged the national security,” he added.

sources.text:
Here's the latest
• CNN reporters denied access: The White House this evening denied two CNN journalists from covering Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s arrival back at the White House for a state dinner, after trying to tell the network which type of journalists could cover the event.
Passes reinstated: Earlier, CNN along with MS NOW and Politico were allowed back into the White House after a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate press badges for the news outlets.
• Judge’s order: The move came after the three outlets told federal Judge Timothy Kelly that their journalists were still denied entry in the morning despite his ruling. Overnight, Kelly had ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate their access after the outlets were banned from the premises last week by President Donald Trump.
CNN White House reporters denied access to Xi's state dinner arrival
The White House on Thursday denied two CNN journalists from covering Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s arrival back at the White House for a state dinner, after trying to tell the network which type of journalists could cover the event.
When a reporter and producer tried to gain access to the event, a press wrangler barred them from entering and told them to “talk to” White House Communications Director Steven Cheung.
Yesterday evening, the White House solicited names for credentials to cover Xi’s arrival. CNN responded with names for a team that included a reporter, producer and camera crew, as is its standard coverage practice for White House events.
About an hour before Xi’s arrival was scheduled, the White House said CNN could cover the event but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, notably excluding the network’s editorial team consisting of a reporter and producer.
Other television networks were permitted to cover the greeting with reporters and producers. CNN told the White House that it wants to cover the event with an editorial presence.
Attorney representing CNN discusses today's ruling on the media ban
Ted Boutrous, the attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico, discusses today’s developments with CNN’s Jake Tapper.
Trump falsely claims CNN "refused to cover" Xi events at White House
President Donald Trump falsely claimed that CNN and MS Now “refused to cover” the arrival of Chinese President Xi at the White House, after reporters for the two networks were not allowed into the White House until about an hour after event was open to the press.
Both CNN and MS Now covered the event on their digital platforms.
“CNN and MSDNC, to show you how fake they are, today refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years, the arrival at the White House of the Highly Respected President of China, Xi Jinping, and his beautiful wife, Madam Peng. The event was magnificent — Actually made for Television but, because they’re Fake News, and because they knew how good it would be, they didn’t want credit to be given to ‘TRUMP,’ they refused to be there,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
CNN's Dana Bash discusses the extraordinary circumstances of Trump's White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico. The three outlets on Thursday afternoon regained access to the White House after the president banned them over the weekend.
Xi arrived at the White House around 10:00 a.m. CNN reporter Betsy Klein was not allowed back into the White House until around noon, after several attempts in the morning.
While access to the White House grounds has since been restored to badge-holders at CNN, MS Now and Politico, the issue of White House TV pool coverage is separate and unsettled. CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox News, which make up the TV pool, are waiting to receive confirmation from the White House that CNN will be allowed to fulfill its pool responsibilities in the future. ABC is pool today and networks are not covering events at the White House for pool until CNN’s status is confirmed.
CNN, MS Now and Politico were denied access to arrivals for the White House state dinner later on Thursday.
Judge sets timeline for next steps in lawsuit, will not hold hearing today
A federal judge declined the request from media outlets that he hold an emergency hearing on the issues CNN, MS NOW and Politico were having accessing the White House Thursday morning.
CNN was allowed back into the White House on Thursday at noon after a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate its access.
In the brief order, Judge Timothy Kelly pointed to a declaration filed by a top White House press officer indicating that press badges were reactivated for journalists at CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Journalists from all three outlets are now inside the White House complex.
In a separate order, Kelly set out the schedule for briefs to be filed on whether he should issue a preliminary injunction in the case.
The media plaintiffs must file a motion for a preliminary injunction by next Monday, Sept. 28.
The administration must reply by October 2, and the plaintiffs can respond by October 5.
A hearing on that request will be scheduled at some point as well, Kelly said, adding that “intends to rule expeditiously.”
Press TV pool is still in a holding pattern
If you’re wondering the reason why you’re not seeing video of President Trump and Xi Jinping, it’s this:
The television pool that usually handles live coverage of Trump’s events is still in a holding pattern due to his unprecedented ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
While journalists for the three outlets are now back at the White House, thanks to a federal judge’s order, the status of the TV pool is a separate matter.
The five major networks that make up the pool — CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC, and Fox News — are waiting on confirmation from the White House that CNN will be allowed to fulfill its pool responsibilities in the future.
At the moment, the pool doesn’t have that assurance, so it has not filmed any of Trump and Xi’s events so far today.
Trump gives away the game with his comment about friendly Chinese reporters
The administration’s lawyers have been arguing in court that President Donald Trump’s attempt to ban media members isn’t about politics, but rather is about national security.
But a comment Trump made during Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s visit would seem to get at his real goal: acquiescence.
According to the White House pool report, Trump “made a joke about how the Chinese had the friendliest press corps.” The Associated Press reported that Trump also remarked on how Chinese reporters ask Xi for permission to speak.
There is, of course, a reason for that. And it’s that China is an authoritarian country with repressive restrictions on free speech and the press.
This isn’t the first time Trump has seemed envious of authoritarian leaders wielding such power. He has frequently praised them.
And he’s made some remarkable comments about how they treat journalists.
Back in 2019 at the G20 summit in Japan, Trump said to Russian leader Vladimir Putin of the assembled press: “Get rid of them. Fake news is a great term, isn’t it? You don’t have this problem in Russia, but we do.”
And in 2015, Trump responded dismissively to a question about the murders of journalists who criticized Putin.
“He’s running his country, and at least he’s a leader, you know, unlike what we have in this country,” Trump said, referring to then-President Barack Obama.
When pressed, Trump ultimately agreed that he would condemn Putin’s crackdown on journalists, saying, “Oh sure, absolutely.”
Trump quips that China has the friendliest press corp
President Donald Trump quipped Thursday that the Chinese had the friendliest press corps during a photo spray with Chinese photographers — the same day the White House repeatedly denied US reporters access to the grounds despite a court order.
“US and Chinese photographers were separated from the pool and brought in for two sprays with the president, according to two of the photographers who were present,” according to a White House print pool report. “During the second spray, Trump made a joke about how the Chinese had the friendliest press corps.”
The pool reporter later sent additional context, saying a person familiar with his remarks said that Trump remarked they were the “friendliest press corps” because “they ask him (Xi) if they can ask a question.”
Chinese state media was at the White House covering Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit. CNN, MS NOW and Politico were repeatedly denied entry after Trump banned the three outlets last week, but were ultimately let back in around noon Thursday due to a court order.
White House tells court that press badges have been reactivated
The head of the White House’s press operation said in a court filing Thursday afternoon that press badges for journalists from the three news outlets that had been banned from the grounds have been reactivated.
The declaration from press shop director Micah Stopperich lays out a timeline for when the White House and Secret Service began complying with a judge’s order to restore access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, although it appears to contradict the on-the-ground experience of journalists.
As late as 11 a.m. ET, CNN and MS NOW journalists were denied entry, however, contradicting the White House’s declaration. All three outlets have now been allowed in, as of 12:29 p.m ET.
According to Stopperich, the White House was notified at 7:10 am ET that it should start restoring access and began the process of reactivating the badges 15 minutes later. Secret Service confirmed the badges were turned back on at 9:07 am ET and began looking for badges that it had confiscated around that time, according to the filing. The confiscated badges were left at the gate entry for pick up at 9:55 am ET.
Judge Tim Kelly had requested that the administration respond to allegations made by the outlets in court Thursday morning that their journalists were still being denied entry to the White House.
Politico gains access to White House grounds
Politico has gained access to the White House grounds after it was earlier denied entry.
Now, all three outlets originally banned by the White House, MS NOW, CNN and Politico, are inside the campus.
Crowd gathers around CNN reporter as she returns to White House grounds
A crowd of press gathered around CNN reporter Betsy Klein as she prepared for her first television appearance moments after she was let back onto the White House grounds, taking photos and videos of the moment.
CNN was allowed back into the White House on Thursday around noon after a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate its access hours earlier. Klein was previously denied access multiple times as she tried to enter the complex on Thursday morning.
CNN allowed back into White House after judge orders Trump admin to reinstate press badges
CNN was allowed back into the White House on Thursday at noon after a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate its access.
Federal Judge Timothy Kelly ruled overnight that the administration’s revocation of press badges from journalists at CNN, MS NOW and Politico was done without “constitutionally adequate due process.”
CNN reporter Betsy Klein was allowed to reenter the White House on Thursday. She was previously denied access despite multiple attempts to enter the complex on Thursday morning. A photojournalist was also earlier denied access.
After some staff were denied entry, CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed an emergency request for a hearing.
It comes after President Donald Trump announced last Friday that he was banning the three outlets from the White House.
Court order to restore media access prompts internal chaos at White House, sources say
Multiple White House advisers and officials said Thursday that they had no idea what the plan was after CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters were repeatedly denied entry to the White House despite a court order — describing a sense of internal chaos.
One official said they had tried to get clarity from senior officials on their stance but questions went unanswered.
“It’s chaotic, no idea,” the official said about potential plans to reinstate the media outlets’ access. Since the court order was issued, a CNN reporter was denied entry to the White House multiple times throughout the day.
Another White House official said they were completely unaware of what was happening. And an adviser to the president echoed that sentiment, adding that they had been unable to get answers on why the reporters were being denied access.
Meanwhile, the timing of the ban is causing angst among Chinese and US officials during leader Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, DC. While the state visit would typically prompt extensive TV coverage, the networks have pulled TV pool duties due to the ban and are largely not airing any video.
Chinese officials had privately expressed concern to some of Trump’s advisers that the current pool ban would negatively impact how the trip was covered, one source told CNN. The issue has also worried White House officials, who know both Trump and Xi wanted robust coverage of the summit, another adviser said.
CNN reporter has once again been denied access to the White House
CNN reporter Betsy Klein tried for a fourth time to access the White House on Thursday but was once again denied entry to the grounds in the last hour.
It comes as lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico requested an emergency hearing after some staff were refused entry to the White House this morning despite a judge’s order for the Trump administration to immediately restore their press badges.
MS NOW also reported that they were denied access again in the 11:00 a.m. ET hour.
President Donald Trump announced last Friday that he was banning the three outlets from the White House.
The Trump administration has frequently tested court orders
The Trump administration has a long history of testing court orders, with dozens of judges finding it has failed to comply with them in the past.
The administration has insisted that it follows court orders. But an Associated Press review back in May found that US district court judges ruled the administration had violated court orders in at least 31 lawsuits over the first 15 months of Trump’s second term. That included cases involving government employee layoffs, spending cuts and deportations.
Perhaps the most prominent example came in March 2025, when the administration failed to abide by US District Judge James Boasberg’s oral order instructing it not to continue with flights deporting Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador. Boasberg found there was probable cause to find the government in criminal contempt, but a federal appeals court later ordered him to end his inquiry. That case is ongoing.
Another US district judge, George W. Bush appointee Patrick Schiltz, found what he said were more than 200 instances of the administration violating immigration-related court orders. He at one point summoned the head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to court for contempt proceedings.
A whistleblower last year also alleged that a former top official in the Trump Justice Department, Emil Bove, told DOJ officials that they may need to consider ignoring court orders. The administration cast doubt on those allegations, but seemed to issue carefully worded defenses.
Bove was later confirmed by the GOP-controlled Senate as an appeals-court judge.
Chinese state media at the White House as three US outlets still denied entry
Chinese state media is at the White House today covering leader Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington while three US outlets request an emergency hearing to regain access to the White House.
CNN witnessed state media on the White House campus today, at one point filing into the press briefing room and taking pictures at the podium.
It comes as some journalists at CNN, MS NOW and Politico are still unable to enter the White House complex despite a ruling that ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate their press badges.
Chinese state media is tightly controlled and the government routinely limits press access. The White House recently downplayed any comparisons between Chinese press restrictions and President Donald Trump’s media ban.
“There is no comparison,” deputy White House press secretary Taylor Rogers told Spectrum News when asked whether the press office has any concerns about the message Trump’s ban sends to China.
Trump admin has "repeatedly violated" court order, media outlets' lawyers say
Lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico said that the Trump administration has “already repeatedly violated the Court’s Order” as they requested a hearing be held “as soon as possible” today.
It comes after the White House denied entry to some of the three outlets’ journalists despite a judge’s order ordering the administration to restore their press badges.
“This morning journalists from each of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO attempted to enter the White House and were turned away,” attorneys for the media outlets wrote, “and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated.”
Conor Fitzpatrick, the chief supervising attorney for the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, said in a statement that the White House refusing Federal Judge Timothy Kelly’s order would be “a dangerous escalation and an affront to the rule of law.”
The request for an emergency hearing comes during a busy news day at the White House. Chinese leader Xi Jinping is expected to arrive to the White House soon, but the major networks comprising the White House TV pool have suspended their normal coverage duties in solidarity with the outlets.
Senate GOP leader says White House needs to “follow the court order” on press access
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday that the White House needs to “follow the court order” when asked about some reporters still being denied entry.
“I think you follow the court order, yeah. I mean, you can appeal. Obviously, there’s a process,” the South Dakota Republican said. “I don’t know if this is a processing issue. I don’t know if that’s been defined yet. But yeah, no, they need to follow the court order.”
CNN, MS NOW and Politico file emergency request for a hearing
CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed an emergency request for a hearing Thursday morning after being refused access to the White House despite a court order.
The news outlets are requesting a new hearing be held in their lawsuit against the Trump administration, after some reporters were denied entry to the White House following Judge Timothy Kelly’s order early Thursday morning temporarily reinstating their access.
Despite Kelly’s order, finding in part that the administration didn’t give notice or an opportunity to appeal the ban before it was announced late last week, some journalists, including two from CNN, were still denied access to the White House.
The White House has not said why it the journalists are still being denied entry.
Some CNN, MS NOW and Politico staff refused entry to White House
Some CNN, MS NOW and Politico staff were unable to gain access to the White House early Thursday morning even after a judge ordered that the Trump administration “shall immediately return, reinstate, and restore” their press badges.
Federal Judge Timothy Kelly said in an order just before 1:00 am Thursday morning that the administration’s revocation of press badges from journalists at CNN, MS NOW and Politico was done without “constitutionally adequate due process.”
CNN reporter Betsy Klein and a photojournalist, however, were denied access to the White House grounds Thursday morning. One CNN producer was able to enter the White House using their pass after 6:00 am. It was not immediately clear why the person was able to enter the building.
Reporters from MS NOW and Politico were also barred from entering the building early Thursday morning, according to the outlets.
The White House has provided no details as to why the journalists were not admitted.
Klein was first denied access to the grounds on Saturday, and her press pass was seized.
It comes after President Donald Trump announced last Friday that he was banning the three outlets from the White House.
Overnight, judge ordered White House to restore access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico
Federal Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately reinstate CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s access to the White House shortly before 1:00 a.m. on Thursday after they were banned from the premises by President Donald Trump.
Kelly found that the revocation of reporters’ press badges was done without “constitutionally adequate due process.”
“The ‘general rule’ is that ‘individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them’ of a constitutionally protected interest,” Kelly wrote in his ruling citing case law.
The Trump administration didn’t notify the reporters of an opportunity to appeal his decision until days after the passes were confiscated.
Trump announced the ban of the three outlets in a social media post Friday, writing that he was kicking the news outlets out “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and adding “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
The three news outlets sued, requesting the ban be paused or blocked entirely. In court filings and during a hearing Wednesday, an attorney for the outlets argued the ban contradicted prior court rulings, violated due process and was issued merely because of Trump’s disdain for the journalists.
Attorneys for the administration countered, saying that Trump’s decision did include an appeals process — one that was only spelled out in letters sent to the outlets days after the ban was announced.
