sources.news_title: UPDATE: CNN, MS NOW and Politico back at the White House, hours after judge ordered Trump to lift ban
sources.text:
NEW YORK — Reporters from three news outlets banned from the White House by President Donald Trump were back on the grounds Thursday afternoon, hours after a federal judge ordered the administration to reinstate their access.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists were allowed back in, the latest development in an extraordinary showdown between Trump and media outlets whose coverage he dislikes. It comes during a heavy news cycle with Chinese leader Xi Jinping visiting with Trump and world leaders gathered for the United Nations General Assembly.
Also Thursday, the news outlets had asked in a court filing for an immediate hearing to address their inability to access the White House grounds earlier in the day. The filing said a Secret Service agent had confiscated the journalists' credentials.
Trump first announced he was banning the outlets Friday, assailing what he called "fake news," and only later arguing that their reporting was a risk to national security. The outlets argued in a joint lawsuit that the ban was a blatant violation of the First Amendment because it singled them out for the content of their coverage.
In his late-night ruling to temporarily strike down the ban, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House to "immediately return, reinstate, and restore" the three outlets' access. He said they had met the legal thresholds to obtain a temporary restraining order, in effect for 14 days, and were likely to succeed in showing that their press passes were revoked without due process.
"This is a high bar, but Plaintiffs have met it," he wrote.
Kelly — whom Trump nominated in 2017 and who ordered a CNN journalist's access restored in a similar case in 2018 — said the government must have clear standards for conduct that would lead to revoking a press pass. He called the standard of objectionable reporting outlined in letters that the White House sent the outlets "so vague it hardly does the trick."
The judge also made clear he did not buy the administration's argument that the news outlets' reporting endangered national security — and noted that Trump himself had not used that argument in the beginning, focusing solely on what he called negative coverage.
"Nothing in the record ... suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns," he wrote.
The ruling came after Kelly heard arguments in an emergency hearing Wednesday. Temporary restraining orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo pending a closer review of the case by the court.
"This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law," Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, said in an emailed statement. "We greatly appreciate the court's swift action."
The White House did not respond to emails from The Associated Press asking for comment on the order.
Attorneys debated access to the White House and any risk to national security
Boutrous argued in the hearing that there was an urgent need for renewed access, saying that the ban caused irreparable harm to the outlets at a time of momentous news events. "We're at war. We have world leaders coming to Washington."
Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik, in his argument, reiterated the administration's point that the president has the right to choose who gets into the White House.
"Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Velchik said.
In arguing that Trump was not engaging in viewpoint discrimination — the government singling out specific media outlets for the content of what they say or publish — Velchik said the president had criticized other news organizations, but not banned them. He noted, for example, that Trump had called ABC "the worst."
He added: "The president should be able to take immediate action to protect national security."
In response, Boutrous said, "Suddenly it's a national security case," arguing that the president brought up that point only after the lawsuit was filed.
Trump "keeps proving our point," Boutrous said, describing how the president has consistently used negative coverage of him as justification for the ban.
Kelly seemed to agree, writing of the national security claim: "Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was 'banning' Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs' reporting."
The Trump administration outlined 'reporting incidents' of each news outlet
In a filing Tuesday, administration lawyers detailed letters sent to each of the three news outlets that identified "a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents, including those that have threatened national security and spread falsehoods."
Among the incidents cited were: CNN reporting on "'top-secret' construction details related to the East Wing bunker"; MS NOW reporting "on an alleged leak investigation"; and Politico publishing "a document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements."
Politico's letter also included an incident in June of a report in which a "senior administration official … granted anonymity" predicted whether a preliminary deal would end the conflict with Iran.
That item appeared to reference a background briefing set up by the White House, where an official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the administration itself. Several other outlets also reported the official's remarks.
Major networks refrained from covering Trump for the media pool
The ban prompted other media outlets to take action in solidarity. The U.S. network press pool — consisting of the five major networks, including CNN — has suspended coverage of Trump pool events pending further notice.
The ruling did not address that rotating pool. After the hearing Wednesday, the networks continued to refuse to air footage of Trump without assurances that CNN would be permitted into the White House pool.
Journalists from Fox News, CBS and NBC were present but not shooting video at Joint Base Andrews, where the president formally welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Other television outlets whose crews were present, according to signs on their tripods and cameras, were NewsNation, Newsmax, Right Side Broadcasting Network, One America News and LindellTV.
Ahead of Wednesday's hearing, an amicus brief was filed by other news groups, including The AP, urging the court to immediately restore the three outlets' White House access.

District Court judge unpersuaded by some of the stupidest arguments ever filed by the Department of Justice
sources.text:
District Court judge unpersuaded by some of the stupidest arguments ever filed by the Department of Justice
Not something you can take for granted these days:
A federal judge has ordered the White House to immediately restore the press credentials of three news organizations after President Donald Trump barred their reporters from the complex last week.
Early Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly granted a temporary restraining order sought by POLITICO, CNN and MS NOW as part of a joint lawsuit filed challenging the revocations. Citing the urgent needs of a “free press,” Kelly ordered the 78 journalists’ credentials returned for at least two weeks while further litigation plays out.
The Trump-appointed judge suggested that the national security grounds the administration claimed to justify the ban amounted to an after-the-fact justification of a decision the president appeared to have made over more mundane disagreements with the outlets’ reporting. Kelly called the disputed stories “routine.”
“The Court is skeptical — at least on this record — that Defendants’ interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes,” Kelly wrote in an eight-page ruling issued just before 1 a.m. Eastern.
“Nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns. Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting,” the judge added.
The judge noted that the administration provided no support for its assertion that any of the disputed stories contained classified information or actually damaged national security and said some of the reporting was months or years old, belying claims the administration’s claims of urgency by the administration.
Kelly’s order rested primarily on due process grounds, so perhaps the administration will have better luck if they promulgate a regulation forbidding reporters with press passes from quoting the vice president.

Journalists for CNN, MS NOW and Politico return to the White House upon judge's orders
Primary Content

White House reporters for MS NOW, CNN and Politico are back in the White House as of midday Thursday, after days of being barred entry because President Trump said the news outlets "purposely write negative news."
In a ruling issued shortly after midnight, U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly for the District of Columbia granted a 14-day temporary restraining order to CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which had press credentials of their journalists covering the White House revoked on Saturday.
Yet early on Thursday, the news outlets said some of their journalists were denied entry to the White House. They asked the court for an immediate hearing. Kelly gave the Trump administration until 12:30 p.m. ET to respond.
In a declaration filed shortly before that deadline, Micah Stopperich, the director of White House press operations, says her team began to work on restoring access after receiving word at 7:10 a.m. The job took just under three hours to complete.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a joint lawsuit against Trump on Monday, on the grounds that revoking their journalists' permanent access to the White House violated their constitutional rights. They sought a temporary restraining order on the ban that would allow them to report from the White House as the proceedings in the case continue.
Kelly, a Trump appointee, wrote that news outlets were "likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process," and on the grounds that "'individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them' of a constitutionally protected interest."
Judge appeared inclined to order the White House to restore access
At an emergency hearing on Wednesday afternoon, Kelly said right off the bat that it appeared the White House had violated the news outlets' constitutional right of due process — which was set out in previous court decisions — when it abruptly blocked the access of journalists who held permanent credentials to work in the building.
Theodore J. Boutrous, a lawyer representing the three news outlets, said the White House ban was a form of retaliation for their coverage of the president, adding that it was "probably the clearest case in history" of viewpoint discrimination.
Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik, on the other hand, argued that access to the White House was a "privilege," not a right. He also cited national security concerns as a reason for the continued ban. In its legal filings, the department had included White House letters to the three news organizations taking issue with stories on a variety of topics, including construction of a "top secret" bunker under the White House ballroom, talks with Iran and whether there were "very bad" vibes at the recent Republican convention in Dallas.
Boutrous pushed back on the claim, asserting that the first mention of national security came only days after the ban was imposed.
" I guess the light bulb went off and they all decided 'Start talking about national security,'" Boutrous said.
Court ruling questions Trump's "actual motivation"
In his Thursday ruling, Kelly said "the court is skeptical — at least on this record — that Defendants' interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes," in reference to White House press credentials.
In its court filing, in response to the lawsuit filed by the three media organizations, the Department of Justice included White House letters, dated Sept. 22, where it accuses the barred media outlets of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."
Judge Kelly argued that the defendants offered no evidence to explain how "any of the reporting they identified in their letters to Plaintiffs damaged national security." He added that the reporters who wrote the stories that the government lawyers identified in their letters to the three media "did not even hold hard passes."
Kelly also wrote that "the record is bereft of any relevant 'formally articulated standards' in place before any of the conduct" for which the reporters had their credentials revoked. He dismissed the examples provided by the White House in the letters to the three outlets as a standard "so vague it hardly does the trick."
Kelly also ruled out the urgency of the case as to deviate from due process.
"Nothing in the record suggests the need for such urgency here," adding that some of the news stories identified in the DOJ notices to the media "stretches back months or years."
"The sorts of stories Defendants identify in the letters to Plaintiffs are routine," he added.

Judge blocks Trump media ban. But for how long?
News outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico will regain access —temporarily — to the White House after a federal judge blocked President Donald Trump’s ban.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, whom Trump appointed, issued a 14-day temporary restraining order early Sept. 24 requiring the administration to restore the reporters’ press credentials while legal challenges continue.
Kelly found that the outlets were likely to succeed on their claim that the administration revoked their access without due process. He also rejected the government’s argument that national security concerns justified the ban.
Trump announced the restrictions Sept. 18. After reporters were turned away from the White House the following day, the organizations sued, arguing that the administration had violated their free speech and due process rights.
The administration has maintained that White House access is a privilege, not a right. In court filings, government attorneys argued that the outlets’ reporting on classified and sensitive information posed national security risks, USA TODAY reported.
The restrictions barred the organizations’ journalists from entering the White House grounds but did not prevent them from reporting on Trump and his administration.
The order does do not resolve the broader legal challenge to the ban but only allows access as it continues to be litigated.
The Trump administration has argued in court that access to the White House is a privilege, not a right, and that the targeted outlets pose national security risks because of their reporting on classified and sensitive information, USA TODAY reported.
Trump lashed out at a CNN reporter and other news outlets in a Sept. 22 Truth Social post, accusing them of having a “Trump addiction.”
“They’re all sick, treasonous, and demented!” he wrote.

CNN, Politico, MS Now regain access to White House after court order
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (CN) — The White House on Thursday reversed course and restored access to journalists from CNN, Politico and MS Now, after several hours’ delay complying with a federal judge’s order blocking President Donald Trump’s ban on the outlets.
In a sworn declaration, Director of White House Press Operations Micah Stopperich wrote that White House Operations were notified at 7:10 a.m. EST to begin restoring access, which they did by 9:55 a.m. EST.
The three outlets said their journalists were then able to enter the White House in time to begin covering Chinese Prime Minister Xi Jinping’s state visit.
Early Thursday morning, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, approved a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to restore press credentials to the outlets and their journalists as the case continued. He noted the clear lack of process in the revocation and rejected the government’s national security claims.
In an eight-page order, Kelly acknowledged national security is a “weighty interest” for the executive branch and judicial review should be “highly deferential,” but he found little evidence to justify the White House’s reliance on those concerns.
“The court is skeptical — at least on this record — that defendants’ interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes,” Kelly wrote.
However, when journalists from the outlets arrived at the White House Thursday morning, they were still denied access. They were admitted to the grounds later in the day.
According to Politico, a Secret Service agent initially told one of its reporters he was not cleared to enter but could use a temporary day pass — meant for journalists without a permanent “hard pass.”
Speaking from the Oval Office Friday, Trump said he ordered the ban because of “one-sided” and “never good” reporting over the last two years and threatened to ban other outlets. The ban stripped journalists of hard passes to the White House, expressly barring them from the entire grounds.
The outlets were also removed from the White House press pool — a rotating group of reporters who share responsibility for video, audio, photography and print coverage of the president — leading other broadcasters in the pool to yank their own coverage of the president in solidarity.
“For one thing, nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” Kelly wrote. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting."
Kelly further rejected the government’s reliance on letters to the news outlets explaining the bans were due, in part, to their use of anonymous quotes from a “senior administration official.” Reporting has shown the quotes were from a press call hosted by the White House. The government argues the quotes raise national security concerns so there was no requirement for full process.
“But the circumstances here are not so ‘extraordinary’ as to permit deviation from the ‘essential principle of due process’ that a deprivation of liberty ‘be preceded by notice and opportunity for hearing,’” Kelly wrote. “The sorts of stories defendants identify in the letters to plaintiffs are routine.”
“Defendants offer no declarations or other support — classified or unclassified — explaining how any of the reporting they identified in their letters damages the national security,” Kelly added. ”The declarations they do provide include general background about classified information, but the declarants are senior officials in the Department of Defense who have no direct knowledge of how reporters operate in the White House, or about any of the facts at issue here."
Kelly highlighted that CNN reporter Betsey Klein’s credentials were revoked months after reporting cited by the government, “undercutting any argument that she or her employer, for example, had the requisite notice that the conduct at issue violated a relevant standard."
Kelly found the journalists were likely to succeed on their claims for two reasons. First, Kelly said he was bound by D.C. Circuit precedent in *Sherrill v. Knight*and *Karem v. Trump,*which require journalists receive due process in disputes over their White House press passes.
Second, the journalists will likely be able to show their credentials were revoked without constitutional due process, as they White House provided neither notice nor an opportunity to be heard before the journalists were stripped of access.
Kelly noted that, under *Karem,*the government can only revoke a White House-issued hard pass if it promulgates a set of rules or standards governing the conduct that would lead to a revocation.
The White House’s arguments that the two D.C. Circuit cases were wrongly decided fail, since until they have been overturned Kelly said he must still follow their rulings.
The news outlets had asked Kelly to schedule an emergency hearing to address the White House’s initial non-compliance. Kelly first ordered the government to explain itself by 12:30 p.m. EST.

sources.news_title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico allowed back in White House after judge orders end to ban
sources.text:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico allowed back in White House after judge orders end to ban
WASHINGTON – All three media outlets that President Donald Trump banned from the White House were allowed back in Sept. 24 after a judge ruled that the revocation of their credentials probably violated the Constitution.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, had ordered the administration to respond by 12:30 p.m. ET. CNN, MS NOW and Politico announced that their reporters were let back in just after noon, though many of them were initially denied access in the morning.
Micah Stopperich, director of White House press operations, submitted a statement to the court that the press credentials were restored Thursday morning and available for retrieval before 10 a.m.
But the legal fight over the media ban isn’t over. Judge Kelly ordered the White House to reinstate the credentials for just 14 days while the news outlets sued over the revocation. But Trump said he expected Kelly to rule against him – and that his administration would appeal.
Trump initially announced Sept. 18 he was revoking credentials for the outlets, accusing their reporters of publishing inaccurate stories and threatening national security. But Kelly found no evidence from before the revocation that the ban stemmed from national security concerns.
Legal battle over White House credentials far from resolved
Even though CNN, MS NOW and Politico have returned to the White House, the legal battle is far from resolved.
Judge Kelly ordered the administration to restore the badges for only two weeks after Trump banned the organizations. Kelly could extend his order so the reporters can continue at the White House while the case is litigated.
But Trump has said he expected Kelly to rule against him and would appeal to a higher court.
The dispute could eventually reach the Supreme Court. Trump accuses the news outlets of threatening national security with poor reporting. But the outlets argue they have a First Amendment right to access if other organizations are granted credentials.
What’s next? Judge sets key deadlines
Judge Kelly set deadlines for the three news outlets and the Trump administration to file written arguments in the dispute over White House credentials.
Kelly told CNN, MS NOW and Politico they must file their request by Sept. 28 for a longer restoration of their credentials than the 14 days he ordered. The Trump administration would have to reply by Oct. 2, and the news outlets could reply by Oct. 5.
Kelly said he would set a date for a hearing on any longer-term order later.
Inside White House, previously banned outlets return to workspace
Reporters from Politico and CNN returned to their workspaces inside the media area of the West Wing shortly after their access was restored.
A Politico reporter was back at the publication’s desk, and several journalists for CNN returned to a small office where the network operates its White House coverage.
Major television networks still haven’t resumed White House pool coverage
Even though Trump’s media ban is no longer being enforced, the White House television pool has not returned to covering the president.
As a result, the five major television networks have not aired video footage from Trump’s meeting with President Xi Jinping Thursday at the White House. Xi is on a multi-day state visit this week in America.
CNN reported the five major networks that make up the pool – CNN, Fox News, ABC, CBS and NBC – are still waiting for confirmation from the White House that CNN will be let back into the pool. Although reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back in the White House earlier in the day, the pool operates separately.
This pool is composed of a small group of reporters from television, print and radio outlets given close face-to-face access to the president during events. The pool includes one network camera crew, which broadcasts a television feed that is shared with other networks.
Critics of media ban say judge’s order ‘not optional’
Critics of the Trump ban called it unconstitutional and said obeying the judge’s order wasn’t optional.
Conor Fitzpatrick, chief supervising attorney for the free-speech advocacy group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, said the administration doesn’t have the option of ignoring the judge’s order.
“Court orders are not optional,” he said. “Refusal to abide by a court ruling has a name: contempt. And contempt has clear consequences.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, said Trump’s “desperate, repressive media ban is flagrantly unconstitutional.”
“No president should be able to use censorship to escape accountability,” Schumer said on the Senate floor. “Is Trump so fragile, so thin-skinned, so desperate that he can’t handle reporting that reflects the truth that he doesn’t want to hear?”
What did Judge Kelly rule overnight?
Judge Kelly said in his order he was restoring the credentials for 14 days because they had been revoked without “constitutionally adequate due process.”
“For one thing, nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” wrote Kelly, who ruled in 2018 against Trump suspending another CNN reporter’s credentials.
Kelly also said he is bound by a 1977 precedent, when a federal appeals court ruled that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny press passes to reporters based on the content of their coverage if the White House has voluntarily opened its doors to media and established facilities for the press.
Trump has said he would appeal the ruling.
The organizations have continued to report on Trump and the White House, but haven’t been allowed on the grounds.

WASHINGTON (TNND) — CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists are back inside the White House after they were denied entry multiple times Thursday morning despite a federal judge’s order requiring the Trump administration to restore their press credentials.
All three outlets were allowed back inside by 12:29 p.m. ET. CNN reporter Betsy Klein reentered the White House after she was repeatedly turned away earlier in the day; a CNN photojournalist was also denied entry before the credentials were reactivated.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily blocked President Donald Trump’s ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House late Wednesday, ordering the administration to immediately restore the outlets’ hard-pass credentials.
“This is a high bar, but Plaintiffs have met it,” Kelly wrote in the order.
The 14-day order directs White House officials to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the hard-pass credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW and Politico that were revoked around Sept. 18.

The legal dispute comes weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, in which Trump’s fellow Republicans are seeking to retain control of Congress. Trump’s job approval ratings have been at record lows in recent opinion polls, amid concerns over issues including the Iran war and inflation.
At a Wednesday hearing, Kelly said two precedents from the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit made clear that journalists are entitled to due process before their White House press passes can be revoked.
He also said it did not appear that the White House had given the targeted outlets a meaningful opportunity to challenge the revocation of their access.
A lawyer representing the news organisations told Kelly that the outlets were banned without the legally required advance notice or an opportunity to contest the decisions, which he described as unprecedented, unreasonable and severe punishments.
A Justice Department lawyer argued that the administration had provided a sufficient explanation for revoking the press passes in letters sent to the outlets on Tuesday. Kelly appeared sceptical of that argument, noting that the letters were issued only after the revocations had taken place and the lawsuit had been filed.
In a legal filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department argued that access to the White House is a privilege rather than an entitlement and that the President has authority to suspend access by news organisations.
A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organisations filed a legal brief on Wednesday supporting CNN, MS NOW and Politico. They argued that stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of their perceived editorial viewpoint violates longstanding US Supreme Court precedent.
Hours after Kelly’s ruling, however, journalists from the three outlets were still denied access to the White House. The organisations sought an emergency hearing, saying their reporters had been turned away despite the judge’s order.

CNN, MS NOW And Politico Return To White House
sources.text:
The standoff over White House press access shifted again Thursday when reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back onto the grounds after a federal judge ordered the administration to restore their credentials.
The White House ban had kept journalists from the three organizations outside the complex for several days, setting up a federal court fight over press access, due process and the First Amendment. According to The Associated Press, reporters from all three outlets were back on White House grounds Thursday afternoon after initially encountering problems entering earlier in the day.
Trump announced the restrictions the previous Friday while criticizing the organizations as “fake news,” according to the Associated Press. The administration later argued that some of their reporting raised national security concerns, while CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued, arguing that they had been targeted because of the content of their journalism.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order directing officials to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the outlets’ access. The order remains in effect for 14 days while the broader lawsuit continues.
“This is a high bar, but Plaintiffs have met it,” Kelly wrote, according to Reuters. Kelly found that the outlets were likely to succeed on their argument that the removal of their credentials violated constitutional due process protections.
The dispute also centered on what standards the government can use when deciding whether to revoke a journalist’s White House credentials. According to the Associated Press, Kelly said officials need clear standards governing conduct that could result in losing access. He described the administration’s stated standard involving objectionable reporting as “so vague it hardly does the trick.”
Kelly also questioned the administration’s national security explanation.
“Nothing in the record … suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” he wrote.
The judge later added, “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting.”
Attorney Theodore Boutrous Jr., representing the outlets, praised the temporary order.
“This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law,” Boutrous said in a statement reported by the Associated Press. “We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
Before reporters ultimately returned Thursday afternoon, the outlets told the court that journalists were still encountering problems accessing the White House. Reuters reported that CNN, Politico and MS NOW requested an emergency follow-up hearing after saying the administration had not immediately complied with Kelly’s order.
During arguments in the case, Boutrous emphasized the importance of immediate access during a packed international news cycle.
“We’re at war. We have world leaders coming to Washington.”
Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik defended the administration’s authority over access.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” Velchik said.
Velchik argued that criticism alone did not prove viewpoint discrimination because Trump had criticized other organizations without removing them. He pointed to Trump calling ABC “the worst.”
“The president should be able to take immediate action to protect national security,” Velchik said, according to the Associated Press.
Boutrous challenged that explanation during the hearing.
“Suddenly it’s a national security case,” he said, adding that Trump “keeps proving our point” through his public comments about coverage from the three organizations.
Administration lawyers had also submitted letters detailing what they described as “a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents, including those that have threatened national security and spread falsehoods.”
According to the Associated Press, those examples included CNN reporting on “‘top-secret’ construction details related to the East Wing bunker”; MS NOW reporting “on an alleged leak investigation”; and Politico publishing “a document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements.”
The administration also cited a Politico report involving a “senior administration official … granted anonymity.” The Associated Press reported that the comments appeared to come from a background briefing organized by the White House itself, during which journalists were instructed to attribute the remarks anonymously.
The White House ban also affected the broader television press pool. Reuters reported that major network journalists had declined to record or distribute certain pooled coverage while the three organizations remained excluded, adding another layer to the dispute over how the White House manages media access.
For now, CNN, MS NOW and Politico have regained access, but Kelly’s ruling is temporary. The lawsuit continues, leaving the court to consider the larger constitutional questions surrounding the government’s ability to revoke established press credentials and whether officials can base those decisions on objections to a news organization’s reporting.

Politico reported one of its reporters had also been granted access.
Earlier Thursday, Kelly granted CNN, Politico and MS NOW a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to restore the outlets’ hard-pass press credentials.
The order requires the defendants, excluding President Donald Trump, as well as their agents and representatives, to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the White House hard-pass press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
Kelly granted the media organizations’ request in the ongoing case Cable News Networks, Inc. v. Trump after their credentials were revoked on Sept. 18, according to the court order.
Kelly expressed skepticism about the Trump administration’s argument that the stories it cited as justification for revoking the outlets’ press credentials raised national security concerns.

He also noted that Trump did not mention national security concerns when he announced the ban.

Boutrous focused on that due process argument near the end of the hearing, telling the court that the White House’s “Alice in Wonderland process” for terminating the credentials is “arbitrary” and “irrational.”

Our previous coverage continues below.
Welp, President Donald Trump was right about a thing.
On Tuesday, Trump appeared to predict via social media that the judge presiding over the lawsuit filed by CNN, MS NOW and Politico over the president’s selective White House press pool ban would ultimately rule in the plaintiffs’ favor and, so far, that’s exactly what’s happening, because, on Thursday morning, the judge ordered the White House to restore the outlets’ access while the case plays out, and expressed skepticism that Trump’s big, babyish ban had any merit at all.
Not exactly a Nostradamus-level prediction, obviously, since courts have ruled that this president and his administration can’t just revoke press access all willy-nilly, but it’s yet another example of the president abusing the power of his office and forcing the judicial branch to step in and stop him.
According to the New York Times, U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly granted a 14-day restraining order and told the White House to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the press credentials held by employees of the three outlets. By the way, the outlets aren’t arguing that their First Amendment rights were violated; they’re arguing they didn’t receive due process to challenge the bans before their access was revoked, and the judge agreed.
From the Times:
The news organizations were likely to succeed in their claim that the White House had violated their constitutional due process rights by revoking their press credentials without advance notice or an opportunity to respond, Judge Kelly wrote in the order issued in the early hours of Thursday.
He also rejected, for now, the administration’s argument that revoking the outlets’ press credentials was necessary to protect national security.
“This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action,” Theodore J. Boutrous, a lawyer representing the media companies, told CNN.
As we previously reported, the White House claimed in a court filing that the three outlets were banned because they were “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information.” It claimed it sent each outlet a letter that included a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” to back up this claim, but the only examples listed in the filings were the funding of Trump’s ballroom and details regarding his East Wing bunker, which the White House described as “top secret,” even though the president has spoken extensively about his pet projects publicly, whether anyone wanted to hear about them or not.
Also, it’s going to be difficult to argue that this ban was about national security when Trump has already made it abundantly clear that he banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico because they “purposely write negative news” about him.
According to the Associated Press, Judge Kelly said in his ruling that the government must have clear standards for conduct that would lead to revoking a press pass. He said the White House’s reasoning for banning the three outlets was “so vague it hardly does the trick.”
I mean, this isn’t exactly an administration that is known for backing up allegations with any semblance of actual substance, so…
And, of course, Kelly pointed out that Trump has already made this ban all about the negative reporting, making the new argument that it’s a security issue quite dubious. (Told you!)
“Nothing in the record … suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” he wrote.
In Trump’s Tuesday tweet, he called Kelly “disloyal” because, no matter how often he’s lost in federal court, he still doesn’t seem to understand that the judicial branch does not answer to him.
Kelly is a Trump appointee, nominated by the president during his first term in 2017. In 2018, Trump revoked the White House press credentials of CNN journalist Jim Acosta after the two got into a heated exchange during a press conference, and Kelly ruled the credentials had to be restored because Acosta hadn’t been given an opportunity to contest the decision. Look, I’ve written before about how Trump is the epitome of what many call the definition of insanity: trying the same thing over and over again, and expecting different results.
Anyway, according to AP, reporters from all three outlets said their access to the press pool was still blocked a few hours after the judge issued his order. MS NOW White House correspondents Laura Barrón-López and Akayla Gardner both reported on air Thursday morning that they still did not have access to the White House.
This, of course, isn’t the first time Trump has defied a judge’s order, only to buckle later. We’ll have to wait and see how it all shakes out this time.
So, this court battle is still ongoing, but things aren’t looking good for our emotionally fragile president. However, things look great for preserving the free press under an administration that keeps attacking it, albeit largely unsuccessfully.
This is what checks and balances look like, and they have been working overtime to keep this administration in check for the better part of the last two years.

The 75-year-old said that he and his wife, Lorrie, felt “shock” and “anger” after receiving the diagnosis in August 2025 and asked the inevitable question: “Why me?” Yet the man remembered for remaining calm as a powerless Airbus descended over New York is approaching the illness with the same refusal to surrender to fear. “It’s as simple as not being afraid. Just not giving up,” he told Robin Roberts in an interview scheduled to air Thursday on “Good Morning America.” Mr. Sullenberger said that if this must be his “last flight,” he intends to go out “using full afterburner.” By sharing the diagnosis, he hopes to make other families confronting Alzheimer’s feel less alone – another attempt, in very different circumstances, to help people reach safety.

Earth has moved beyond seven of the nine “planetary boundaries” that scientists use to measure whether the natural systems supporting life remain within a safe operating range. The latest planetary-health assessment, prepared by 60 scientists led by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, found that climate change, the loss of biological diversity, changes to land and freshwater systems, disrupted flows of nitrogen and phosphorus, the introduction of novel entities such as synthetic chemicals and plastics, and ocean acidification have all crossed safe limits. The danger is not that mankind falls from a cliff the moment a line is crossed. Rather, every breach weakens the forests, oceans, soils, and other systems that steady the climate and sustain food and water, increasing the chance that one change will amplify another and become irreversible. Only the boundaries covering the ozone layer and atmospheric aerosols have improved over the past decade, evidence that collective action can still move a global indicator in the right direction. Scientists nevertheless warned that the Amazon rainforest may be approaching a tipping point at which large areas can no longer sustain themselves – a change whose effects would reach far beyond South America.

A proposed ban on U.S. diesel exports could lower prices briefly – and then make the shortage worse. Republican lawmakers facing anger from farmers and truckers have urged Mr. Trump to restrict exports after average U.S. diesel prices rose above $6 per gallon amidst disruptions to refineries and fuel shipments caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine. The United States is the world’s largest diesel exporter, so keeping more fuel at home could initially increase domestic supply. Refiners and energy analysts warn, however, that export markets help keep American refineries operating at high volume. If producers lose those buyers, they may reduce output or postpone investment, leaving less diesel available and pushing prices higher over time. An export ban would also tighten supplies abroad, raise transportation and food costs, invite retaliation from trading partners, and disrupt contracts with countries that depend upon U.S. fuel. The Trump administration has thus far resisted the proposal, although the political pressure is growing as the harvest and home-heating seasons approach and voters prepare for the midterm elections.

The Philippine Senate lowered the number of votes needed to convict Vice-President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial, ruling that the constitutionally required two-thirds majority should be calculated from senators who remain legally and factually able to participate rather than from all 24 members of the chamber. Thirteen senator-judges voted to overturn an earlier ruling that fixed the threshold at 16 votes; the presiding officer cast the sole vote against the change, while six members of the minority did not participate. Four senators are currently unable to take part because they are detained, in hiding, or on medical leave, meaning that the revised standard could reduce the number required for conviction to 14. Ms. Duterte is accused of misappropriating public funds, amassing “unexplained wealth,” and plotting to “assassinate” senior officials including President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. She denies the charges and calls the proceeding politically motivated. A conviction would remove her from office and could bar her from seeking the presidency in 2028, when she is expected to be a leading candidate. Her lawyers said that they may challenge the threshold ruling before the Supreme Court.

Mr. Trump signaled a major retreat on Tuesday in his quest for European real estate. He signed an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the U.S. military presence on the world’s largest island and permits new bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, as well as a “Golden Dome” missile-defense installation. But the agreement explicitly stops short of conveying any territory to the United States. Denmark, which governs the vast green but largely empty space, very much wants the world to be aware of that distinction. Mr. Trump first raised the possibility of buying Greenland from Denmark during his first term and never quite let go of the idea. Now, instead of an acquisition on the scale of President Thomas Jefferson’s Louisiana Purchase, Mr. Trumphas secured a larger U.S. military presence while galvanizing European allies against his administration.

sources.news_title: Judge Blocks Trump Administration From Banning News Organizations From White House
sources.text:
WASHINGTON—A federal judge today temporarily blocked the Trump administration from barring CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House press facilities. The decision by U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly came in a lawsuit filed by the news organizations against President Trump and three advisors after the administration banned the outlets from the White House and confiscated their reporters’ press credentials. The Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University joined the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (RCFP) in filing an amicus brief in support of the news organizations earlier this week.
The following can be attributed to Jameel Jaffer, executive director, Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University:
“We welcome Judge Kelly’s order. Trump’s ban harms both the press and the public, which relies on journalists to report independently on the president and his administration. We hope that Judge Kelly will soon make his temporary order permanent, and that his permanent order addresses the news organizations’ First Amendment claims, not just their Fifth Amendment ones. The First Amendment bars the president from transforming the press corps into a propaganda machine.”
The Knight Institute and RCFP’s amicus brief argues that the press has, for over a century, fulfilled a crucial role by reporting on newsworthy events from within the White House on behalf of the American people, and that the president’s decision to ban news organizations from the White House based on the viewpoints expressed in their reporting violates the First Amendment. Read the brief here.
Read today’s temporary restraining order here.
Read more about the case, CNN v. Trump, here.
The Knight Institute has supported the Associated Press in its challenge to its exclusion from the White House, filing three separate amicus briefs over a period of 18 months. The Institute has also supported The New York Times in its challenge to restrictions on access to the Pentagon. Earlier, the Institute successfully sued President Trump over his blocking of critics from his Twitter account, which the Institute argued was a “public forum” for First Amendment purposes.
